newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian parliament, cabinet clash over reform.
newsitem.headline: Russian parliament, cabinet clash over reform.

text.p: Russia's reformist government and the communist-dominated parliament skirmished on Tuesday over ministers' plans to kick-start a stagnating economy and repair public finances by slashing social benefits.

The State Duma, or lower house, rejected a package of bills prepared by the cabinet to cut or scrap most of the welfare benefits which served as a complex safety net under the Soviet system but have become too heavy a burden for the new Russia.

The government says that more than 100 million Russians, two thirds of the population, receive various benefits, including tax breaks and subsidies on rent and other housing costs exceeding 350 trillion roubles ($60 billion) a year.
"No economy can handle that much," Interfax news agency quoted Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Sysuyev as saying.

President Boris Yeltsin, worried by growing discontent over falling living standards, brought young and ambitious reformers into the cabinet in March and gave them a virtually free hand to give a new impetus to stalled market reforms.

The reformers, led by youthful first deputy premiers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov, have vowed to sweep away the remnants of the Soviet era paternalistic centralised system to encourage private initiative and promote an effective market economy.
But first the new government team needs to plug a yawning gap in the budget which threatens overall economic stability.
Ministers see proposals to scrap welfare benefits as the first step toward more dramatic reform of the welfare system, saving at least 30 trillion roubles ($5.2 billion).
Duma leaders oppose the government's economic plans, saying they would further raise tensions in the country and ultimately lead to violent social unrest.
But neither side appeared overly excited by Tuesday's vote.
RIA news agency quoted communist Duma speaker, Gennady Seleznyov, as saying that the entire problem was in the poor quality of the proposed drafts rather than in the general idea.
Sysuyev told Interfax that he still hoped the Duma would pass the bills before going into summer recess on June 24.

"It's a very delicate game in which everyone saves their trump cards for the decisive moment and no one is keen to trigger unnecessary consequences," one government official told Reuters, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Government and parliament are bracing for bigger battles over government bills to be considered before the Duma recess.

One of them is the new tax code, which the cabinet hopes will make investment in the Russian economy more attractive by cutting red tape. Another is a plan to cut spending in the 1997 budget because of lower-than-expected tax revenues.
The government, for its part, is pressing hard to squeeze overdue taxes out of major corporate debtors and put huge natural monopolies under stronger government control.
Chubais' spokesman Andrei Trapeznikov told Reuters that the government was threatening to force one of its biggest oil producers, Nizhnevartovskneftegaz, into bankruptcy.
Both sides of the tug-of-war nevertheless realise that there are limits which they may not break without serious risks.
They are waging a war of nerves, with deputies feeding rumours about a possible vote of no confidence in the government and ministers making veiled threates about dissolving the Duma.
"There is little chance that these threats will be carried out in deed," the government official said.
The Duma, if it tries to oust moderate Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, could very well see Chubais or another liberal simlarily hated by the communists as Yeltsin's new choice.
Yeltsin, if he decides to call early Duma elections, could end up with an even more hostile parliament given widespread public dismay with unpaid wages and pensions at present.
"Everyone seems to realise how high the stakes are and the main thing now is not to overpress," the official said.
